content.title: Average Value and Net Change in Calculus
content.overview: This lesson covers two fundamental applications of the definite integral: calculating the average value of a continuous function over a closed interval and determining the net change of a quantity given its rate of change. These concepts are essential for interpreting physical and mathematical models in AP Calculus BC.
learning_objectives: Calculate the average value of a continuous function over a closed interval [a, b].
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to find the net change of a quantity from its rate of change.
Interpret the units and physical meaning of average value and net change in context.

sections.title: The Average Value of a Function
sections.content:
For a continuous function f(x) on the interval [a, b], the average value is defined as the integral of the function over the interval divided by the width of the interval. Mathematically, this is expressed as: Average Value = (1 / (b - a)) * ∫[a to b] f(x) dx. The units of the average value are identical to the units of f(x). Conceptually, this represents the height of a rectangle with width (b - a) that has the same area as the region under the curve f(x).

![A linear sequence showing the steps to find the average value: Identify interval a, b, Set up integral of f(x), Evaluate definite integral, Divide by (b - a), and Verify units.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/c2278ab9-a62b-4425-bff4-df4fcc21f32b-1786519384034-810.webp)

sections.title: The Net Change Theorem
sections.content: The Net Change Theorem states that the integral of a rate of change is the net change in the original quantity. If R(t) is the rate of change of a quantity Q(t), then the net change from t = a to t = b is: Q(b) - Q(a) = ∫[a to b] R(t) dt. Unlike total distance or total accumulation of absolute values, net change preserves the sign of the rate. A positive result indicates an overall increase, while a negative result indicates an overall decrease. The units of the result are the units of the quantity Q.

sections.title: Verification and Interpretation
sections.content: When communicating results, always include units. For average value, verify that the result lies between the minimum and maximum values of the function on the interval (Mean Value Theorem for Integrals). For net change, ensure the sign of the integral correctly reflects whether the quantity increased or decreased over the time period.

worked_examples.question: A hypothetical model describes the temperature T(t) in °C over 24 hours as T(t) = 18 + 3·cos(πt/12). Find the average temperature on the interval [6, 18].
worked_examples.solution:
1. Identify the interval: a = 6, b = 18. The interval length is 18 - 6 = 12.
2. Set up the average value integral: (1/12) * ∫[6 to 18] (18 + 3·cos(πt/12)) dt.
3. Find the antiderivative: 18t + (3 * 12 / π)·sin(πt/12) = 18t + (36/π)·sin(πt/12).
4. Evaluate at the bounds: [18(18) + (36/π)sin(18π/12)] - [18(6) + (36/π)sin(6π/12)].
5. Simplify: [324 + (36/π)sin(3π/2)] - [108 + (36/π)sin(π/2)] = [324 - 36/π] - [108 + 36/π] = 216 - 72/π.
6. Divide by interval length: (216 - 72/π) / 12 = 18 - 6/π.
7. Final Answer: Approximately 16.090 °C.

worked_examples.question: The net rate of water flow into a tank is given by R_net(t) = 0.8 - 0.5·sin(πt/6) m³/hour. Calculate the net change in volume from t = 6 to t = 18.
worked_examples.solution:
1. Set up the definite integral of the rate: ∫[6 to 18] (0.8 - 0.5·sin(πt/6)) dt.
2. Find the antiderivative: 0.8t + (0.5 * 6 / π)·cos(πt/6) = 0.8t + (3/π)·cos(πt/6).
3. Evaluate at the bounds: [0.8(18) + (3/π)cos(18π/6)] - [0.8(6) + (3/π)cos(6π/6)].
4. Simplify: [14.4 + (3/π)cos(3π)] - [4.8 + (3/π)cos(π)].
5. Since cos(3π) = -1 and cos(π) = -1: [14.4 - 3/π] - [4.8 - 3/π] = 14.4 - 4.8 = 9.6.
6. Final Answer: The net change is +9.6 m³, indicating an increase in volume.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide by (b - a) when calculating the average value.
Using the absolute value of the rate (total distance/accumulation) when the question specifically asks for net change.
Incorrectly applying the chain rule in reverse when finding the antiderivative of trigonometric functions (e.g., forgetting the reciprocal of the constant inside the sine/cosine).
Omitting units or using the units of the rate for the net change result.
exam_tips: Always show the definite integral setup with bounds before evaluating.
Round final numerical answers to three decimal places as per AP standards.
Check that your average value is 'reasonable'—it must be between the function's minimum and maximum on that interval.
Distinguish between 'average value of f' and 'average rate of change of f'; the latter is a slope (difference quotient).
content.recap: To find the average value of a function, integrate it over [a, b] and divide by the interval length. To find the net change of a quantity, integrate its rate of change over [a, b]. Always verify units and ensure the sign of the net change reflects the direction of change.

knowledge_claims.content: The average value of a continuous function f on [a, b] is defined as (1 / (b - a)) times the definite integral of f from a to b.
The Net Change Theorem states that the definite integral of a rate of change R(t) from a to b equals the total change in the quantity Q(b) - Q(a).
The units of the average value of a function f(x) are the same as the units of f(x) itself.
The units of the net change of a quantity are the units of the quantity itself, not the units of its rate of change.
The average value of a continuous function on an interval [a, b] must be a value between the absolute minimum and absolute maximum of the function on that interval.
Net change is the signed integral of a rate, whereas total distance or total accumulation is the integral of the absolute value of the rate.
To calculate net change, one must find the antiderivative of the rate function and evaluate the difference between the antiderivative at the upper bound and the lower bound.
A common error is confusing the average value of a function with the average rate of change, which is calculated using the slope formula (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).
A positive net change result indicates that the quantity increased over the interval, while a negative result indicates a decrease.
If a tank has an inflow rate f(t) and an outflow rate g(t), the net change in volume is the integral of the net rate (f(t) - g(t)).
The interval length (b - a) used in the average value formula represents the width of the domain over which the function is being averaged.
When integrating trigonometric functions like cos(kx), the antiderivative involves multiplying by the reciprocal of the constant k (i.e., 1/k).

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Average Value and Net Change — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.
options.B: Arc Length of Parametric and Vector Curves: Arc length accumulates speed, using the square root of the sum of squared component derivatives.
options.C: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.
options.D: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Average Value and Net Change — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.B: Average Value and Net Change: The average value of a function divides its integral by interval length, while net change integrates a rate with signs preserved.
options.C: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.
options.D: Derivative as a Limit: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
